title: Pride, the last thief
hook: ahankar is the last and hardest thief

segments.voice: Yesterday, anger: the burning thief that pushes compassion out of the chair. Your line was breathe first. Did one breath come before one word? Day one thousand four hundred one.

A whole morning in the gurdwara shoe room. Rows of sneakers and sandals, wiped and set straight, handed back with a smile. Real seva, done well. Then the drive home, and a small thought slips into the passenger seat: not everyone would have done that. Nothing loud. Just a warm little glow, a quiet tally. The other thieves need some kind of opening. Anger needs an insult. Greed needs something shiny. This one walked in through the good deed itself. Today: pride, ahankar, the thief the title calls the last.
screen: `A MORNING OF SEVA IN THE SHOE ROOM.` → `NOT EVERYONE WOULD HAVE DONE THAT.` → `PRIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Ahankar: pride, the swollen I, the self puffed up and asking to be seen. When the Granth names the five thieves, it lists them as lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride. Pride closes the list. Second, why it's the hardest. Every other thief can be fought, and the fighting itself can feed this one. Beat your anger and you can grow proud of your calm. Give up greed and you can grow proud of your simplicity. Even humility can turn into a trophy. That's one way to read the title: the last thief is the one still standing after you've beaten the others, because it lives on the beating. Third, the Guru's mirror. In the Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan says it in one sharp line, in paraphrase: whoever calls himself good, goodness does not come near him. Not, goodness leaves him. It never comes close. The moment a person crowns themselves, the crown is all that's left. Fourth, the hope. In Asa di Var, in a salok of Guru Angad, the Second Guru, the Granth speaks of haumai, the ego that sits under pride, and says, in paraphrase: ego is a long, deep disease, but its cure is also within it. The same self that swells can bow. The Gurus' cure is grace and the Name, remembered again and again, and the kind of seva that's done and then forgotten. So back to the shoe room. The seva was good. The tally on the drive home is the thief. The way through isn't to stop serving. It's to catch the tally, smile at it, and hand the credit back to the One who gave the hands.
screen: `AHANKAR: THE SWOLLEN I.` · `IT FEEDS ON BEATING THE OTHERS.` · `CALL YOURSELF GOOD, GOODNESS STAYS AWAY.` · `THE CURE IS ALSO WITHIN.` · then, large: `THE LAST THIEF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: catch one proud thought. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last day or two for something you did well. Then look for the little glow that came after it, the quiet tally: I'm the one who, at least I, not everyone would. Don't scold it. Just catch it, the way you'd catch a cat on the kitchen counter, gently, and set it down. On each out-breath, hand the credit back. If you pray, you can thank the Lord for the hands that did the work. The bell holds the time.
Pride. Ahankar, the swollen I, the thief that can feed even on victories over the others; the Gurus say its cure is also within. Today's word.
Your line: the last thief. Today, after you do something good, watch for the tally that follows, and when you catch it, quietly hand the credit back. Day one thousand four hundred one.

howItsDone: Sikhs name ahankar, pride, among the five thieves and counter it with nimrata, humility, through Naam Simran and seva, such as cleaning shoes and serving langar in the gurdwara.
